'''Mumble''' is a [[voice over IP]] (VoIP) application primarily designed for use by [[Gamer|gamers]] and is similar to programs such as [[TeamSpeak]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/FAQ#What_is_Mumble.3F |title=FAQ/English – Mumble |publisher=www.mumble.info |access-date=2011-06-30 |archive-date=2014-12-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141224151518/http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/FAQ#What_is_Mumble.3F |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Mumble uses a [[client–server]] architecture which allows users to talk to each other via the same server.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/FAQ |title=FAQ/English – Mumble |publisher=www.mumble.info |access-date=2011-06-30 |archive-date=2014-12-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141224151518/http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/FAQ |url-status=dead }}</ref> It has a very simple administrative interface and features high sound quality and low [[Latency (audio)|latency]]. All communication is encrypted.<ref name="potm">{{cite web|url=https://sourceforge.net/blog/potm-200911/ |title=Project of the Month, November 2009 |publisher=SourceForge.net |date=2005-08-31 |access-date=2011-06-30}}</ref>

Mumble is [[free and open-source software]], is [[cross-platform]], and is released under the terms of the [[BSD licenses|BSD-3-Clause]] license.<ref name="license" />

== Channel hierarchy ==
A Mumble server (called '''Murmur''') has a root channel and a hierarchical [[Tree structure|tree]] of channels beneath it. Users can temporarily connect channels to create larger virtual channels. This is useful during larger events where a small group of users may be chatting in a channel, but are linked to a common channel with other users to hear announcements. It also matches team-based [[first-person shooter]] (FPS) games. Each channel has an associated set of groups and [[access control list]]s which control user permissions. The system supports many usage scenarios, at the cost of added configuration complexity.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/ACL_and_Groups |title=ACL and Groups/English – Mumble |publisher=www.mumble.info |access-date=2011-06-30 |archive-date=2020-09-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200909190359/https://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/ACL_and_Groups |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Sound quality ==
Mumble uses the low-[[Latency (engineering)|latency]] audio codec [[Opus (audio format)|Opus]] as of version 1.2.4,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://blog.mumble.info/mumble-1-2-4-released/|title=Mumble 1.2.4 released {{!}} Mumble|website=blog.mumble.info|language=en-US|access-date=2017-09-30}}</ref> the codec that succeeds the previous defaults [[Speex]] and [[CELT]].  This and the rest of Mumble's design allow for low-latency communication, meaning a shorter delay between when something is said on one end and when it's heard on the other. Mumble also incorporates [[echo cancellation]] to reduce echo when using speakers or poor quality sound hardware.

== Security and privacy ==
Mumble connects to a server via a [[Transport Layer Security|TLS]] control channel, with the audio traveling via UDP encrypted with [[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES]] in [[OCB mode]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/FAQ/English#Is_Mumble_encrypted.3F|title=FAQ/English - Mumble Wiki|access-date=2015-06-12|archive-date=2014-08-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140826115650/http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/FAQ/English#Is_Mumble_encrypted.3F|url-status=dead}}</ref> As of 1.2.9 Mumble now prefers [[Elliptic curve Diffie–Hellman|ECDHE]] + [[Galois/Counter Mode|AES-GCM]] cipher suites if possible, providing Perfect Forward Secrecy.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://blog.mumble.info/mumble-1-2-9/|title=Mumble 1.2.9 - Mumble Blog|access-date=2015-06-12}}</ref> While password authentication for users is supported, since 1.2.0 it is typically eschewed in favor of strong authentication in the form of public key certificates.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/Features#Authentication|title=Features - Mumble Wiki|access-date=2015-06-12|archive-date=2015-06-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150613202048/http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/Features#Authentication|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Overlay ==
There is an integrated overlay for use in fullscreen applications.<ref name="potm" /> The overlay shows who is talking and what linked channel they are in. As of version 1.0, users could upload avatars to represent themselves in the overlay, creating a more personalized experience. As of version 1.2, the overlay works with most [[Direct3D]] 9/10 and [[OpenGL]] applications on Windows and has [[OpenGL]] support for Linux and Mac&nbsp;OS&nbsp;X.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/Games#Overlay |title=Games – Mumble |publisher=www.mumble.info |access-date=2011-06-30 |archive-date=2020-11-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112023712/http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/Games#Overlay |url-status=dead }}</ref> Support for DirectX 11 applications was later added.

== Positional audio ==
For certain games, Mumble modifies the audio to position other players' voices according to their relative position in the game.<ref name="potm"/> This not only includes giving a sense of direction, but also of distance.

To realize this, Mumble sends each player's in-game position to players in the same game with every audio packet. Mumble can gather the information needed to do this in two ways: it either reads the needed information directly out of the memory of the game or the games provide it themselves via the so-called link plugin interface.

The link plugin provides games with a way to expose the information needed for positional audio themselves by including a small piece of source code provided by the Mumble project.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/Link |title=Link – Mumble |publisher=www.mumble.info |access-date=2011-06-30 |archive-date=2014-08-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140826120027/http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/Link |url-status=dead }}</ref> Several high-profile games have implemented this functionality including many of [[Valve Corporation|Valve]]'s [[Source (game engine)|Source Engine]] based games (''[[Team Fortress 2]]'', ''[[Day of Defeat: Source]]'', ''[[Counter-Strike: Source]]'', ''[[Half-Life 2: Deathmatch]]'')<ref>{{cite web|url=http://store.steampowered.com/news/9221/|title=Updates for Team Fortress 2, Day of Defeat: Source and Half-Life 2: Deathmatch}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://store.steampowered.com/news/9893/|title=Counter-Strike: Source Update Released}}</ref> and ''[[Guild Wars 2]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://forum-en.guildwars2.com/forum/info/updates/Game-Update-Notes-February-26-2013|title=Guildwars Website|access-date=2014-02-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170922072537/https://forum-en.guildwars2.com/forum/info/updates/Game-Update-Notes-February-26-2013|archive-date=2017-09-22|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/Games#Positional_audio|title=Games - Mumble Wiki|access-date=2014-08-24|archive-date=2020-11-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112023712/http://wiki.mumble.info/wiki/Games#Positional_audio|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Mobile apps ==
Third-party mobile apps are available for Mumble, such as Mumble for iOS, Plumble for Android (F-Droid, Google Play, Note: Discontinued in 2016), and Mumla (F-Droid, Google Play).

== Server integration ==
Mumble fits into existing technological and social structures. As such, the server is fully remote controllable over [[Internet Communications Engine|ZeroC Ice]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ostatic.org/blog/interview-mumble-does-oss-voip-chats-for-online-games |title=Interview: Mumble Does OSS VoIP Chats for Online Games |publisher=Ostatic.org |access-date=2011-06-30 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727154500/http://ostatic.org/blog/interview-mumble-does-oss-voip-chats-for-online-games |archive-date=2011-07-27 }}</ref> User channels as well as virtual server instances can be manipulated. The project provides a number of sample scripts illustrating the abilities of the interface<ref>{{cite web |url=http://mumble.git.sourceforge.net/git/gitweb.cgi?p=mumble/mumble;a=tree;f=scripts |title=SourceForge – mumble/mumble/tree – scripts/ |publisher=Mumble.git.sourceforge.net |access-date=2011-06-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120304015232/http://mumble.git.sourceforge.net/git/gitweb.cgi?p=mumble%2Fmumble%3Ba%3Dtree%3Bf%3Dscripts |archive-date=2012-03-04 |url-status=dead }}</ref> as well as prefabricated scripts offering features like authenticating users using an existing [[phpBB]] or [[Simple Machines Forum]] [[database]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://gitorious.com/mumble-scripts/mumble-scripts/trees/master/Authenticators |title=Tree for mumble-scripts in Mumble scripts |publisher=Gitorious |access-date=2011-06-30 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120709025347/http://gitorious.com/mumble-scripts/mumble-scripts/trees/master/Authenticators |archive-date=2012-07-09 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The murmur server uses port 64738 [[Transmission Control Protocol|TCP]] and [[User Datagram Protocol|UDP]] by default. The port number refers to the address of the reset function on a [[Commodore 64]].

An alternative minimalist implementation of the mumble-server (Murmur) is called uMurmur.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://github.com/umurmur/umurmur|title=GitHub - umurmur/umurmur: Minimalistic Murmur|website=[[GitHub]] }}</ref> It is intended for installation on [[embedded devices]] with limited resources, such as, for example, [[residential gateway]]s running [[OpenWrt]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://wiki.openwrt.org/doc/howto/umurmur |title=uMurmur – Howto |publisher=wiki.openwrt.org |access-date=2011-10-09}}</ref>

== Server hosting ==
Like many other VoIP clients, Mumble servers can be both rented or hosted locally. Hosting a Mumble server locally requires downloading Murmur (included as an option in the Mumble installer) and launching it. Configuring the server is achieved via editing the configuration file. The configuration file holds information for the server's name, user authentication, audio quality restrictions, and port.

Administering the server from within requires a user to be given administrator rights, or can also be done by logging into the SuperUser account. Administrators within the server can add or edit rooms, manage users, and view the server's information.
